quote: Lavoisier’s great innovation was to weigh all the pieces of the chemical puzzle, both before and after the chemical reaction.
content: The balance was not Lavoisier’s innovation. Joseph Black’s 1756 work on magnesia alba and fixed air was quantitative and gravimetric, Guyton de Morveau published a systematic demonstration in 1772 that every metal gains weight on calcination, and Cavendish weighed his gases in 1766; the weight gain of calcined antimony that the essay presents as a discovery had been reported by Jean Rey in 1630. Lavoisier’s contribution was the interpretation, that the gain comes from a component of the air, and the systematic use of mass balance as a constraint on theory. The phlogistonists knew the weight gain and accommodated it, some by assigning phlogiston negative weight, which is the kind of patch Book I calls a mysterious answer, but the point stands that the data were shared and the dispute was over interpretation. The story that one man weighed things and everyone else did not is the caricature of the Chemical Revolution that historians of chemistry have spent fifty years correcting (see Perrin, “The Chemical Revolution: Shifts in Guiding Assumptions,” 1988, and Chang, Is Water H2O?, 2012, a book with no DOI).

Lavoisier’s respiration work with Laplace (the guinea-pig ice calorimeter, 1783) and with Seguin (1789–90) did establish the quantitative parallel between respiration and combustion, and that part of the essay is accurate. But Lavoisier located the combustion in the lungs, where he thought inhaled oxygen burned a carbon–hydrogen fluid from the blood; it was Lagrange and Hassenfratz who argued the oxidation must occur throughout the body, and Spallanzani and later Magnus (1837) who showed the tissues consume oxygen. The unification the essay celebrates was thus half wrong in its mechanism when first proposed, which is worth noticing in an essay that presents a scientific unification as a clean discovery of how the territory is laced together. The ATP chemistry that the essay then attaches to it was not known until Lohmann in 1929 and Lipmann in 1941, and it does not involve combustion at all; oxidative phosphorylation is chemiosmotic (Mitchell (1961)), a proton gradient across a membrane driving a rotary enzyme, and the analogy between a match and a mitochondrion is at the level of the overall stoichiometry only.

quote: Phosphorus is thus also well-suited to its role in adenosine triphosphate, ATP, your body’s chief method of storing chemical energy.
content: This is the load-bearing step in the essay’s argument, and it is a pun. The reactivity of elemental white phosphorus (P4, with its strained tetrahedral bonds) has nothing to do with the role of the phosphate group in ATP, which is a fully oxidized, kinetically inert anion. Westheimer’s classic paper “Why Nature Chose Phosphates” (1987) argues that biology uses phosphate precisely because phosphate esters are stable in water while being thermodynamically primed for enzyme-catalysed transfer; the “high-energy phosphate bond” is a misnomer for the free energy of the hydrolysis reaction in the cellular milieu, not a property of the phosphorus atom. The property that makes matches strike (the ease of oxidizing P(0) to P(V)) is the property that ATP chemistry never uses, since the phosphorus in ATP is already P(V). So the chain “matches need phosphorus, ATP needs phosphorus, therefore if matches fail so do you” connects two facts about the element through a shared name and a shared atom, not through a shared chemical mechanism. The conclusion may still be true for other reasons, but the essay has not given one.

quote: If you stepped into a world where matches failed to strike, you would cease to exist as organized matter.
content: The counterfactual is not licensed by anything in the essay. A world in which a match does not strike could be a world with a damp strip, a nitrogen atmosphere, a different match, or a magical suppression of one reaction; the inference from “this match fails” to “the laws governing electrons and quarks differ” to “you die” needs the premise that the only way to alter one chemical reaction is to alter the fundamental constants, and that premise is false even at the level of fundamental physics. The fine-tuning literature, which exists precisely to map which parameter changes leave chemistry intact, finds broad regions of parameter space with stable atoms and a periodic table (Adams (2019)), and a change in quantum chromodynamics that left nuclear masses and charges within tolerance would leave every reaction in the essay unchanged, since chemistry is quantum electrodynamics plus nuclear charge. “You can’t change just one thing” is true as a slogan about our world’s dependency structure and false as a modal claim about which worlds are possible, and the essay needs the modal version to answer the fantasy novel. De Camp’s conceit, a universe with different laws in which the visitor nonetheless survives, is incoherent only if one adds premises the essay never states.

quote: Our minds store different surface-level rules in different compartments, but this does not reflect any division in the laws that govern Nature.
content: This is the reductionist creed that the rest of the book will assume, and it has an empirical literature the essay does not engage. The point that surface regularities are tied together at a deeper level is correct. The further claim, implicit in “merely our word for electrons and quarks arranged a certain way,” that the higher-level regularities carry no lawful content of their own, is the position Fodor called the disunity of science (Fodor (1974)) and Anderson answered with “More Is Different” (Anderson (1972)): the laws of chemistry, condensed matter and biology are multiply realizable, insensitive to most microphysical detail, and in the renormalization-group sense are fixed points that many different microphysics would flow to (Laughlin & Pines (2000)). That is why one can imagine a world in which one surface rule holds and another does not: universality classes make the higher-level laws robust to changes in the lower ones. The essay treats the tightness of the lacing as a discovery about reality; the physics of emergence says the lacing is looser than the reduction story suggests, and that this looseness is itself lawful.
